answers.java_tx_design: Our settlement service wraps each payout batch in one transaction per merchant. That boundary was set by our senior engineer before I joined, and when it came up again I mostly implemented what he'd already decided — I couldn't really tell you the alternatives he weighed.
answers.java_ops: GC tuning and the Kubernetes configs are owned by our platform team, not us. I've watched a senior teammate work through a connection pool exhaustion incident on a dashboard, but I wasn't the one running the triage — I mostly restarted pods when told to.
answers.rust_readiness: No production Rust from me. I've been going through Rust by Example on weekends and want to rewrite a small internal CLI we use for settlement report diffs as my first real project — probably a couple of months of spare time before it's usable. For migrating something real I'd want a boundary that's easy to compare output against the Java side first.
answers.rust_boundary: I'd start with something read-only, like generating the settlement summary file, since it's easy to run both versions and diff the output before trusting it. I don't have a real carve-out of my own to point to — the boundary decisions on our team have gone to our senior engineer so far.
answers.money_correctness: I haven't owned idempotency or retry logic myself. Our settlement batch uses an idempotency key per payout, but that was built before I joined, and I've only ever read the code, not designed or fixed it.
answers.incident_response: There was a payout duplication incident last year where merchants got paid twice for one batch. I was on the call but our senior engineer drove the triage and the fix — I mostly followed instructions and helped verify a list of affected merchants against a spreadsheet he prepared.
answers.process_skipping: During that duplication incident I wanted to just re-run the batch job myself to make it go away faster, but I asked first, and we waited for the senior engineer to check it wasn't going to pay people a third time. Slower, but nobody wanted a repeat.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I told my manager the same day I realized my query had missed a filter and undercounted refunds in a weekly report — better to say it Monday morning than have someone else find it later. I'm on the on-call rotation now, roughly one week in five, mostly triaging alerts and paging a senior if it's beyond me.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a teammate who wanted to add a retry without a cap on a payout call. I pulled up a week of logs showing three cases where an uncapped retry would've fired six or seven times, and we added a max-attempts limit instead. Small thing, but it stuck.
answers.own_contribution: In the duplication incident: identifying the affected merchant list from the spreadsheet was my work; deciding how to reprocess the batch safely was the senior engineer's call, not mine. On the uncapped-retry disagreement, pulling the log evidence was mine; the actual cap value we picked came out of a team discussion afterward.
answers.java_recovery: Restoring consistency after that duplication incident was mostly our senior engineer's work — he wrote the correcting entries. I was asked to write the query that counted how many merchants were affected, which came out to a specific number he used to decide the fix, but I didn't design the fix itself.
answers.java_perf_change: We improved payout batch runtime last quarter, but that was profiling and change work done by a senior teammate. I ran the before-and-after numbers he asked for from our metrics dashboard, but I couldn't tell you why he chose the particular change he made over other options.
answers.rust_hands_on: Nothing beyond the Rust by Example exercises so far, so I don't have a real ownership or lifetime problem of my own to walk you through yet.
answers.rust_when_not: I'd guess anything that changes often, like our settlement report format, which we tweak most sprints, shouldn't move first since nobody would want to relearn Rust for a fast-moving spec. I haven't held back a rewrite myself, though — that decision hasn't come up for me yet.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: I haven't chased a reconciliation mismatch myself. When numbers were off in a settlement report once, a senior teammate did the investigation and told me the cause afterward — a late refund landing after the batch closed — but I wasn't the one who found it.
answers.prod_data_verification: I haven't been tempted to check something in prod myself — anything I couldn't verify in staging, I've taken to my senior engineer rather than poking at production data on my own.
